newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: SLOVAK GOVT FACES PROTEST WAVE BEFORE VOTES.
newsitem.headline: SLOVAK GOVT FACES PROTEST WAVE BEFORE VOTES.

text.p: Slovakia's nationalist government, criticised in the West for dragging its feet on democratic reform, is facing a new wave of popular discontent ahead of two crucial referendums in May.

A strike by actors over alleged government interference in the arts has become a focus of protest against the coalition headed by Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar, involving students, some Roman Catholic bishops and President Michal Kovac.

The protests, the most visible challenge to Meciar's rule since he was elected in 1994, come as Slovakia is preparing for referendums on whether to join NATO and on whether the president should be elected by direct popular vote.

"This activity for the referendum is part of the common protest atmosphere against this government," said Bratislava University professor of political science Miroslav Kusy, a former parliamentary deputy and anti-communist dissident.

The row has also highlighted how sensitive is the issue of culture in a state which has only been independent since 1993, particularly ahead of the referendums, which analysts say will help define Slovakia's place in Europe.
"They are pre-occupied with understanding, believing, having a confidence in Slovak statehood," said one Western analyst in Bratislava.
The actors' strike, which has closed most Bratislava theatres and others, was sparked by the sacking last year of the director and artistic director of the National Theatre.
Government officials say the actors and students are being manipulated by the opposition. Ministers have also cited the need to protect national culture.
But things came to a head last week when Culture Minister Ivan Hudec called in police to end a sit-in at his ministry by actors and supporters, including opposition parliamentarians.
Kovac, locked in a long-running political feud with Meciar, last week added his voice to calls for Hudec to quit.

In a further challenge to the three-party government, he has also called for votes in favour of NATO membership and a change to the constitution to allow direct presidential elections, a move bitterly opposed by Meciar.
Kusy said the current row could affect the outcome of the two referendums to be held together on May 23 and 24.

Kovac's term expires in March and, under the current system, with parliament unable to agree on a new president, Meciar would assume presidential powers until parliamentary polls in September or October.

"There is a fear that after the term of the president expires, power will be concentrated in the hands of the prime minister maybe for a year and this is a very big danger for democratic institutions and the democratic process," Kusy said.

Government officials say Slovakia wants to be among the first new members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) but its chances seem to have slipped after U.S. and European Union criticism of the pace of democratic reform.

Some analysts say the NATO referendum, which asks if voters support membership and whether they favour nuclear weapons or foreign troops in Slovakia, is phrased to elicit a vote against as cover for failure to make the first wave.
But the Western analyst said Slovakia, despite its problems, still belonged with the European democracies.
"I do not think it would be a conscious turning back from being a member of the family of democracies, it would be more a reflection of still defining themselves."
